body.v: Your premium statement for this year is available.
You can also get to it by opening the app yourself.

hotspots.explain: The address ends in helveticare.example, the real domain.
Your first name is a nice touch, but it's the domain that tells you who sent it.
The link text and the real address both lead to helveticare.example.
It reminds you that you can go through the app, without the link.

who.prompt: Who is really writing to you? Read the address, not just the name.
who.answer: HelvetiCare: the address is on helveticare.example, and the link points to the same domain.
choices: A scammer who copied the display name
A broker who bought your data

emotion.prompt: Which feeling is this email pressing on?
emotion.answer: None. A calm notice, with no deadline.

ask.prompt: What does it actually want you to do?
ask.answer: Nothing in particular: a link to read your statement, with no sign-in or payment asked for.
choices: Nothing: it offers a link to a statement

verify.prompt: How can you check through a channel you control?
verify.answer: Open the HelvetiCare app yourself. The email suggests it too: you don't need to trust the link.
choices: Reply and ask for a paper copy
Forward it to a friend for advice

actions.label: Open the HelvetiCare app yourself and read the statement
actions.consequence: The statement is there, as announced.

actions.label: Click the link in the email to read it
actions.consequence: The link goes to the real site: no harm done. Opening the app yourself is still the better habit.

actions.label: Ignore it and read the statement later
actions.consequence: The statement is waiting for you in the app.

attacker_reveal: Put it next to my fake: same sender name, same first name up top, a link in the same place. Except here the domain belongs to the insurer and nothing is rushed. The domain was the thing to read.
